newsitem.title: ITALY: Vacationing VIPs go to Italy, others stay home.
newsitem.headline: Vacationing VIPs go to Italy, others stay home.

text.p: While rock stars, royalty and other rich and famous VIPs flock to sunny Italy for their summer holidays, Italians themselves and less prosperous foreigners are increasingly staying away.
According to a new survey published on Wednesday, Italy's tourism industry is having a bad summer with fewer people going to its resorts and spending less when they get there.

Foreigners, scared off by the strengthened lira, are largely staying away and only Tuscany, with its rolling hills, exclusive beaches and famous Chianti wine, is seeing a rise in oversees tourists, the survey by two business confederations found.
But Italy, and especially Tuscany, is proving a magnet for Europe's elite to escape the stresses of their jet-set lives.
According to Italian newspapers, Britain's Prince Charles fled there in June for a few days with mistress Camilla Parker-Bowles.

Others who chose Tuscany included Princess Margaret, Charles's aunt, John Kennedy Junior, the son of the late U.S. president, British Prime Minister Tony Blair, French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and German opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine.

Celebrities including singer Sting, film stars Tom Cruise and wife Nicole Kidman and Clint Eastwood all regularly holiday in Tuscany and pop star Whitney Houston was in the southern Italian island of Capri earlier this year.
Ordinary tourists, on the other hand, are in decline.
The poll, conducted by business confederations Fipe and Confcommercio, found that tourist demand had contracted by an average 11 percent from May to mid-August compared with 1996.
Fewer tourists were heading to the seaside -- numbers were down by some 20 percent on the picturesque southwestern Amalfi coast -- and 15 percent fewer were holidaying in the mountains.
Only Italy's "art cities" such as Florence were attracting more tourists than last year. Demand there was up 1.6 percent.
"Even compared with 1996, an unhappy year for tourism because of the bad weather conditions and consumer pessimism, things aren't going well at all," Fipe head Edi Sommariva said.

"Italian families, having been hit by the Eurotax, have preferred to change their car this year, thanks above all to the state incentive scheme, leaving just the loose change in their piggy banks for a short holiday," he said.
Italy's economy is showing tentative signs of recovery and the car incentive scheme, which makes it cheaper for consumers to trade in their old cars for new ones, has been a big success.
But taxes, including the unpopular Eurotax aimed at ensuring Italy a place in the single European currency, remain high.

The survey found little enthusiasm even for the coming long public holiday weekend, traditionally the high-point of Italy's summer season. Beach resorts and discotheques are forecasting a fall in attendance of 25-30 percent, it said.
City officials estimate that two in three residents of Turin and more than half those of Bologna will be staying at home during the Friday-Sunday "Ferragosto" holiday.
Bad weather in the mountains -- nearly 100 climbers have died in the Alps already this summer, partly because of bad conditions -- has also discouraged tourists.
Only a strong rise in the number of Russian holidaymakers bucked the trend. "But that's not enough to compensate for the drop in Japanese and Germans," the survey concluded.
